How I work with AI

Rules I bring to every project

  1. 01

    Write the system before the thing

    A story bible before the novel, a 16-section prompt before the screenplay, a walkthrough of how the work is really done before the app. The system is what makes the result repeatable.

  2. 02

    The model drafts, code decides

    In business software the AI reads and suggests, while prices, totals and matching are computed in code, and a person approves every change.

  3. 03

    Ship the whole arc

    A product is not done at the demo. Tests, a walkthrough, a pilot pack, and notes for the next AI session all ship with it.

items.title: Conflion
items.lede: Full-function software for running a law firm, built on a conflicts check and new-matter intake. One system on the firm's own server now covers matters and docketing, documents, time and billing, firm accounting links, people and CLE, client relationships, legal holds, the general counsel's office, IT and facilities, and a firm-wide AI layer that suggests while a person decides.

From a conflicts desk to the whole firm

Conflion began as conflicts and intake, and that is still where every matter starts. It now runs the rest of the firm on the same clients, matters and people, with one set of permissions applied on the server and one firm inbox that lists every decision waiting on each person, with a short morning brief for their role. The firm keeps its systems of record (billing, ledger, HR, document and device systems) and Conflion connects them.

Matters and docketing

A matter workspace with stages, tasks and a record timeline. Court deadlines counted from the rules for California, New York, Texas, Florida, Illinois, Nevada and federal appeals, each step citing its rule, with court notices read into the docket for a clerk to confirm and two-way sync with Outlook or Google calendars.

Documents

Matter folders made at opening, check-out and check-in with version comments, a profile on every document, email filed to a matter from Outlook, and saved searches for each person.

Time, billing and accounting links

Time entry with suggested task codes, pre-bills, bill review, invoices, LEDES exports, collections and a pricing desk. Approved journal entries post to the firm's own ledger in QuickBooks Online, Xero or Sage Intacct, with vendor bills, a bank feed, payroll imports, a cash forecast and partner draws.

People and CLE

One record per person from the HR export, bar admissions and CLE reminders, time away with cover, reviews and feedback, associate development, recruiting, joiners and leavers, and a book test drive for lateral hires before any offer.

Client relationships

Contacts and every conversation with them, key clients with account plans, feedback at matter close, events, mailing lists with consent, panels and RFPs, referral sources and a client portal. A contact is never mixed into the conflicts records.

Risk and the general counsel's office

Claims and incidents against the firm, insurance renewals, ownership due diligence on clients, a risk register and a promise ledger. Legal holds with acknowledgements and reminders, and a file destruction review that a hold always stops.

The office

An IT help desk, a register of the devices and software each person holds, meeting rooms, visitors, post and couriers, and off-site boxes tied to their matters. A leaver's laptop sits on the same checklist as their files and holds.

Knowledge and practice support

"Who has done this" from the firm's own matters, a clause bank with fallback positions and review dates, precedents, closing sets and signature packets (Conflion never signs), privilege logs and productions, and a staffing board.

Ask Newton and the AI tools

One question box for the firm whose answers link to the records behind them, and tools that watch the work: matter pulse, an obligation calendar, an early case read, a client risk radar on public sources, bench notes and rule change watch. Each shows its sources, and a person decides.

The problem

Before a firm takes a matter, it must check every party against everyone it has represented or opposed. Mid-size firms usually search their billing system letter for letter, so they miss parent companies, former names, nicknames and misspellings. Intake is a web form nobody connects to the search, and the enterprise tools are quote-only and installed by consultants.

The people involved have different needs. An associate submits the request, a conflicts analyst reviews the hits, practice leaders and general counsel approve, and finance opens the matter. Conflion gives each of seven roles its own view.

How the matching works

  • Names are normalized: corporate suffixes stripped, abbreviations expanded, initials collapsed so "A.B.C. Holdings" finds "ABC Holdings".
  • Three scorers combine: a phonetic key (Smith and Smyth), Jaro-Winkler for typos, and trigram overlap for spacing. Rare words weigh more than common ones.
  • People match on surname first, then first name with 30+ nickname pairs (Kate and Katherine), aliases and former names.
  • Strong matches expand two hops through corporate families and one hop through personal links such as spouses and officers.

Decisions that come from knowing the work

Risk follows the relationship

A name match alone means little. Being adverse to a current client on an open matter is high risk; a closed matter is medium; a match only through a personal link is capped below high. Related parties with no matter history are dropped as noise.

Rules are built in

Former clients point to Rule 1.9, prospective clients to Rule 1.18, lawyer relationships to California Rule 1.7(b) and (c) disclosures. Lateral hires get the 1.10, 1.11 and 1.12 analysis, and engagement letters check the California fee-agreement statutes.

Lawyers decide, software suggests

The local AI pre-sorts hits and drafts memos, but every AI-filled field carries a mark until a person confirms it. Restricted and walled data never reaches the model, and accepting a suggestion never decides a hit.

Least privilege by role

Approvers see a summary and a sign-off. Requesters see no firm records while they type. Walls are enforced in what the server sends each user, and every blocked attempt is logged.

An audit trail that proves itself

The log is append-only with a hash chain and a "Chain intact" check, and database triggers refuse edits. Matters cannot close until the final bill is issued and trust is at zero.

Speed for the analyst

J and K move between hits, 1 to 5 record a decision, Enter accepts the suggestion, and earlier decisions on the same party appear inline.

Under the hood: scale, outside data and a private model

Conflion now has about 279,000 lines of TypeScript (about 223,000 of source and 56,000 of tests), 3,554 passing tests across 237 test files, and 360 click-through checks that drive the real app in a browser before each batch of changes is merged. It runs two ways from the same code: a browser-only demo on fictional data, or a firm server with its own database, single sign-on, email and an AI model on the firm's own hardware.

Built for a firm with millions of names

Row-level storage, incremental sync and server-side search replaced loading everything into the browser. A repeatable benchmark on synthetic firms goes up to 3,000,000 parties, with a written account of what limited a large firm and what changed.

Outside entity data, watched nightly

A party can be linked to its public-register record: legal-entity data and SEC filings, including subsidiaries read from the latest annual report. A person chooses which names and parents or subsidiaries to add. A nightly job lists what changed for a person to accept or set aside, and cleared requests are flagged for another look.

Search that shows its coverage

Every search gets a number and shows what it covered. An empty or missing source is never shown as clearance, hits carry plain labels such as "likely same entity" instead of scores, and a no-match result is neutral, not green.

Faster hit review

A compact hit list with sticky party headers, identity review kept apart from the conflict assessment, and follow-ups tracked until resolved. The suggested order is learned locally from the firm's own past decisions, shows its factors and counts, is off by default, and never hides a hit or records a decision. An offline evaluation of the ranking is written up in the repo.

Confidentiality and lateral hires

Confidential matters are searched in batch without being revealed: the user is told there is a confidential match and nothing more. Lateral hires get a pre-start checklist with distinct pending, blocked, not-applicable and complete states, each backed by evidence.

Compliance records

Required documents per request, a summary of each conflict, and tracking for business-associate agreements, joint-representation consents and founder acknowledgements.

Measured speed

  • Name search (median): 77 ms to 1.3 ms at 50,000 parties; 535 ms to 5.3 ms at 250,000.
  • Submitting an intake: 1.5 s to 37 ms at 50,000; 8.0 s to 20 ms at 250,000.
  • After a colleague's change, a browser downloads 1 KB instead of reloading 200 KB.
  • Server memory at 250,000 parties: 5.4 GB down to 1.8 GB.

All figures come from a benchmark script run on synthetic firms.

A model that stays on the firm's hardware

The AI runs through Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible local server, so client names never leave the building. It triages hits with a short reason, finds parties in a matter description or pasted email (any name that is not in the text is discarded), drafts a conflicts memo from the recorded decisions only, and suggests column mapping for imports. Every use is written to the audit log with the model name. The ranking model is a separate local statistical fit that uses no AI provider.

Teaching and testing inside the app

  • Role-based walkthroughs (open a matter, prepare a request, approve, clear, get your firm live) that point at things but never click, submit or decide.
  • A first-week checklist that ticks itself off from what the person actually does, with tests that limited roles are never shown a step for a page they can't open.
  • A test environment on a fictional firm, marked by a striped banner on every page. It never writes to live data, sends email or calls an outside AI provider.

Support without sharing firm data

An administrator builds a support bundle of counts, settings switches, versions and error messages with names replaced by placeholders, reads it, then saves it. Nothing is sent automatically, and saving is written to the audit trail. To see a problem happen, support uses a test firm of made-up records at the same size and shape. The live app opens empty, with no sample data, and the desktop app ships for Windows, macOS and Linux with a first-run setup.

Taking it to market

  • Research. 14+ competitors compared from public sources, and 21 gaps ranked.
  • Pilot. Five firms over 90 days in four phases, measured on intake-to-cleared time, analyst hours per check and hits the old system missed.
How it was built

It began as the Conflicts Desk prototype in Claude Code, with tests and CI, and grew into Conflion. I supplied the domain: how conflicts departments actually run, which rules apply, and where existing tools fall short. Claude built the search engine, the synthetic firm and every screen. It then helped research competitors, price the product, write the pilot pack and script and animate the pitch. From there I mapped every area of a firm against what Conflion covered and directed the build of each missing one, from docketing and documents to people, client relationships, the general counsel's office and the office itself, with each area's privacy rules set before its screens.

items.title: VigilMark
items.lede: A trademark watch and triage desk for a conflicts-first law firm: it ranks new filings that look like a client's mark, checks whether the applicant is related to a firm client, and hands the hit to Conflion as an intake.
items.body_html:
Screenshots below

The problem

Trademark watch services flag new filings, but someone still has to decide which hits matter, check whether the applicant is related to an existing firm client (opposing a client's subsidiary can be a conflict of interest), and turn the hit into an engagement before the 30-day opposition window closes. Those three steps usually sit in different tools and inboxes.

What it does

  • Triage feed of incoming Official Gazette and §2(d) hits, ranked by score and days left, filterable by registry.
  • Watched marks portfolio with classes, goods and services, registries and watch strategy.
  • Clearance lab: type two marks and see the scores update live.
  • Enforcement studio: from any hit, a client pitch email with flat-fee options, a cease and desist letter, notice-of-opposition grounds, and an intake file.
  • Batch import of Gazette filings as CSV, JSON or XML, each scored against every watched mark.

How it connects to Conflion

A published contract

VigilMark defines a versioned schema, conflara.intake.v1, that maps a trademark hit onto Conflion's intake: client, matter, related parties and party roles such as parent entity, lead investor and adverse counterparty subsidiary.

Conflict check first

Before it recommends anything, VigilMark checks the applicant and its parent against a watchlist of firm clients and their corporate families, and marks the hit Cleared, Subsidiary review or Direct conflict, always flagged for human verification.

Loosely coupled

One click sends the hit, its scores and the conflict result into Conflion as a signed webhook. The two products share a versioned schema, not a database, so either can change inside without breaking the other. A toggle runs it standalone or in bridge mode.

Scoring you can explain

There is no model call. Sight is an edit-distance similarity. Sound compares phonetic consonant skeletons, so CONFLARA and KONFLARA both reduce to the same letters. Those combine into a mark score, which is blended with a goods-and-services score built from exact class matches, coordinated class groups and shared description vocabulary. Every score comes with a written rationale, which matters for legal work. The app's own labels say "AI"; this is plain algorithmic scoring.

Built to run anywhere

  • Standard-library Python backend with a local database, and a single-file web app that also works straight from disk.
  • A native Mac wrapper that starts the server and opens the app in its own window.
  • Live trademark lookups with rate-limit tracking when an API key is present, and a built-in sample index when it isn't.
How it was built

Built with Google Gemini, which wrote the web app, the Python server, the Mac wrapper and the schema. I set the idea and the Conflion hand-off.

items.lede: A strategy studio for the people deciding where a law firm should use AI. It maps every idea by where the demand came from and how much it changes the work, scores it with honest ranges, ranks the portfolio under different strategies, and carries the winners through pilots.
items.body_html:

The problem

Every firm now has a list of AI ideas, from vendors, partners and its own innovation team. The list is usually ranked by enthusiasm. Ideas with no evidence look as good as proven ones, the loudest request wins, and nobody can explain afterward why one pilot was chosen over another.

What it does

  • A portfolio briefing that opens with a sentence a managing partner can repeat, and rule-based insights that each show the rule behind them.
  • Seven-criterion scoring with confidence ranges. A missing score is never treated as favorable, and thin evidence widens the range.
  • Scenario rankings (balanced, quick wins, differentiation) that state their assumptions and show how each idea moves between them.
  • Side-by-side comparison, a pilot board, a stakeholder map and editable strategy briefs that export to Markdown and PDF.
How it was built

A native macOS app in SwiftUI and SwiftData that runs entirely on the Mac, with optional local (Ollama) or Claude assistance that shows the exact text before anything is sent. I set the brief and the design bar: white, editorial and calm enough for a partners' meeting. Claude Code wrote the app, its scoring engine and the demo portfolio, and built it on my Mac through Remote Control.

items.title: LexAtlas
items.lede: A legal intelligence graph for conflicts, diligence and investigations. It shows how companies, funds, people, matters and sources connect, ties every connection back to evidence, and enforces ethical walls in the data itself.
items.body_html:
Take the guided tourScreens from the running Mac app, with a fully fictional dataset

The problem

Conflicts and diligence questions are graph questions: is this fund related to our client, who controlled this company in 2023, how is this buyer connected to that target? Firms answer them from spreadsheets and vendor feeds that disagree, with no record of which source said what, and with walled matters that can leak through a search result or a count.

What it does

  • A graph explorer and path finder that answers "how are these two connected" within the records the user is cleared to see.
  • Evidence on every edge, with rule-based confidence that always gives its reasons, and disputed, stale or inferred links drawn differently.
  • Time travel: the graph as of any date, and what began or ended between two dates.
  • Ethical walls in the data layer, reversible entity resolution, saved investigations and a cited brief that exports as Markdown, PDF and JSON.
How it was built

A native macOS app in SwiftUI over system SQLite, with an offline graph canvas and optional local or Claude assistants that are off by default. I wrote the specification package; Claude Code built the app and its synthetic dataset and ran the builds on my Mac through Remote Control. The working default is a quiet white workspace, and its eleven other skins live only in Settings.

items.lede: A legal AI assistant for the Mac, built on Claude. Lawyers keep each matter's documents together, ask questions and get answers cited to the page and paragraph, run review tables, redline drafts, check citations and count deadlines, and nothing reaches the cloud until they approve it.

The problem

Big-firm legal AI platforms are powerful but priced and deployed for big firms, and most general chat tools give answers a lawyer cannot check. A smaller practice needs the same core moves, ask, review, draft, verify, with every answer traceable to the record and a clear line on what client data leaves the building.

What it does

  • Matters that hold PDFs (with OCR), Word, Excel, PowerPoint, email and more, read and split into passages on the Mac.
  • Cited answers and review tables across many documents, with each quote located in Skippy's own copy and marked verified or not.
  • Drafting with redlines, exported to Word with tracked changes, and multi-step workflows such as a due diligence report or a chronology of facts.
  • Cite Check, Deadlines and public research through CourtListener, the Federal Register, eCFR and SEC EDGAR.
How it was built

A native macOS app in SwiftUI with no third-party packages. It calls Claude through the Messages API, using citations on per-passage documents, structured outputs and prompt caching, or runs on the user's own Claude subscription, and works offline with local search when neither is available. A Confidentiality Shield can mask names before anything is sent. I set the goal and chose the extra features; Claude Code built it and ran the builds on my Mac.

items.title: Win your case ASAP
items.lede: A litigator's first read of a new complaint, done in minutes. It ranks every theory that could end the case by how early it can be filed, puts each one on the response clock, and quotes the complaint for every point it makes. Run blind on 26 California federal cases decided after the model’s training cutoff, the ground that actually won made its top three in 14, and 357 of 358 quotations checked out word for word.
items.body_html:
Try the demoSaved runs on this site; live analysis runs inside Claude

The problem

The cheapest way to win a lawsuit is to end it early: an anti-SLAPP motion, a demurrer, a motion to compel arbitration, a statute of limitations defense. Those windows open and close in the first weeks after service, often before anyone has read the complaint closely with that question in mind. Miss one and a case that could have ended in month two runs for years.

What it does

  • Ranked theories: each with the motion that carries it, the date it can be filed, the authority, what the client must supply, the other side's best answer, and how far it gets (ends the case, narrows it, or moves it).
  • A response clock built from the forum's own rules, such as the 60-day anti-SLAPP window or the 30-day state response deadline, with dates exportable to Outlook.
  • A claim-by-theory grid showing which theory reaches which claim, first moves for this week, and checkpoints a lawyer must confirm.
  • A whole case file: PDFs, Word files and emails, read in passes when the file is large, and a draft motion outline or memo on request.

Tested against what actually happened

For each case the tool read only the complaint, as of filing, without the outcome. Its ranked theories were then scored against what the court actually did.

26 cases the model could not have seen

California federal cases decided after the model’s training cutoff, so it could not have known how they ended. Each was scored against the court’s ruling.

The winning ground in its top three, 14 of 26 times

Each ranked theory was scored against what the court actually did, from a complaint read as of filing, without the outcome.

Quotes that check themselves

Across the 26 cases, 357 of 358 quoted passages were found word for word in the complaint.

Decisions behind it

  • Earliest first. Theories are ordered by when they can be filed and how much of the case they end, because the value is in the weeks saved.
  • Code checks the model. Deadlines come from coded forum rules, and every quote is matched against the source text in the browser.
  • A lawyer decides. Each theory lists the facts a lawyer must confirm before relying on it, such as whether the plaintiffs actually signed an arbitration agreement.
  • Model choice. Opus, Sonnet or Fable, with a depth setting, so a team can trade speed against thoroughness.

Built to run where lawyers already work

It is a single page that runs inside Claude on the user's own account, so it needs no new vendor, server or install. Large case files are read in 140,000-character passes, two at a time; only facts whose quotes verify are carried forward to one final ranking pass. The real cases use public complaint text and public rulings, with sources linked in the tool.

How it was built

Built with Claude Code as a page that calls Claude for the analysis. I set the goal, an early exit from every case, and the test: run it blind on real complaints, including ones decided after the model’s cutoff, and score it against what the court actually did. Claude wrote the page, the forum rules and the demo matters, found the public cases, and wrote up each scorecard for me to review.

items.title: Testimony Check
items.lede: Feed it the documents in a case and a witness’s sworn statements, and it finds every place the story breaks, with the exact quotes on both sides and a deposition script that walks the witness into the admission.
items.body_html:
Try the demoSaved runs on this site; live analysis runs inside Claude

The problem

Depositions are won on the contradictions, and finding them means holding a declaration, an email thread, a performance file and a chat log in your head at once. Associates do it by hand over days, and a missed contradiction is not recoverable once the witness has been prepared and sworn.

What it does

  • Ranks contradictions as case-ending, major or useful, and flags which statements were made under oath.
  • Shows both sides with the exact quote and the document it came from.
  • Predicts the way out: what the witness will say to explain it away, and how to close that exit.
  • Writes the deposition script as commit, confront and close questions, and lists what not to ask.
  • Takes a real case file: upload documents or paste in your own.

Decisions behind it

  • Quotes are checked by code. Every quoted passage is matched word for word against the source document in the browser, and anything that does not match is flagged.
  • Order matters. The kill shot is one admission, the sequence to get it, and why it ends the issue.
  • A lawyer decides. It prepares the examination; it does not decide what to ask.

What the recorded run showed

It read 13 documents in 256 seconds and found 9 contradictions, 3 of them case-ending, with all 32 quotes verified. In a mock deposition where Claude played a coached witness, the scripted questions produced the key admission at question 8.

How it was built

Built with Claude Code as a page that calls Claude for the analysis. I set the idea and the test; Claude wrote the page and prompts, and a script recorded the run shown here.

items.title: Citation Gate
items.lede: A first-pass screen that runs before the citator check. Every case cited is looked up in a database of real opinions, every quotation is matched word for word against the court’s text, and Claude reads the actual opinion to judge whether it says what the brief claims.
items.body_html:
Screenshots below

What it checks

Citations and quotations, against an index of about 256,000 opinions from CourtListener’s free public data (California Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, Ninth Circuit and U.S. Supreme Court, snapshot of September 30, 2026). It is built to sit beside a citator: the attorney verifies every authority before filing.

The problem

Courts have begun sanctioning lawyers for citations to cases that do not exist, quotations that are not in the opinion, and holdings that say the opposite. The risk grows as more drafting is assisted by AI, and an associate cite-checking at midnight is the only barrier.

What it does

  • Extracts every authority from a brief: cite, pin cite, quotations and the proposition each is cited for.
  • Looks up each case in a local index built from CourtListener, and flags a citation that belongs to a different case.
  • Matches every quotation against the opinion text, word for word, and marks the words that differ.
  • Reads the opinion to judge whether it supports the point, and routes anything uncertain to a lawyer.
  • Signs off: a table a lawyer signs, exported as a file or CSV. The sign-off states that every authority was also checked on KeyCite or Shepard’s.

Decisions behind it

  • Lookup first, model second. Existence and quotation checks are plain code against real text; the model only judges support.
  • No text, no pass. A case with no opinion on file is marked for a lawyer and never passed.
  • Say what it did not check. Statutes and rules are listed as not checked, and even a clean result is stamped “no issues found, citator check still required.”

What the recorded run showed

On a 7-case brief with problems planted, it blocked all four: two made-up or mismatched cases, one misquote and one wrong proposition. It found no problem with the two accurate citations, which still need a citator check, and sent the rest to a lawyer rather than guessing.

How it was built

Built with Claude Code as a page that calls Claude for the analysis. I set the idea and the test; Claude wrote the page and prompts, and a script recorded the run shown here.

items.title: Guideline Guard
items.lede: Every client’s outside counsel guidelines, enforced on each prebill before it leaves the firm. Claude reads the guidelines, audits each line, quotes the rule it applies and proposes the fix.
items.body_html:
Try the demoSaved runs on this site; live analysis runs inside Claude

The problem

Clients now send guidelines that decide what they will pay: who may bill, at what rate, how entries are written, which tasks are never billable. Finance finds violations after the invoice is rejected, weeks later, when the work cannot be corrected and the write-off is already coming.

What it does

  • Extracts a rulebook from the client’s guidelines, each rule with its category, a test and the exact sentence it comes from.
  • Audits every entry as payable, rewrite, reduce, not payable or confirm.
  • Quotes and verifies the rule behind each finding in the page.
  • Proposes narratives that meet the rule, and writes a note to the billing partner.
  • Exports to CSV for the billing team.

Decisions behind it

  • Before the invoice, not after. It runs on the prebill export, when the entry can still be fixed.
  • No new vendor. It runs on the firm’s existing Claude and a billing export.

What the recorded run showed

It extracted 36 rules and audited the 32-entry prebill, finding that $19.3k of the $26k in fees would be cut or questioned as submitted and $7.8k of that was recoverable by rewriting or attaching approvals.

How it was built

Built with Claude Code as a page that calls Claude for the analysis. I set the idea and the test; Claude wrote the page and prompts, and a script recorded the run shown here.

items.title: Hour Catch
items.lede: Every hour you work gets billed. It reads a lawyer’s day across Outlook, Teams, document history and the phone log, writes the time entries they forgot, and runs each one through Guideline Guard before it reaches billing.
items.body_html:
Try the demoSaved runs on this site; live analysis runs inside Claude

The problem

Time that is worked and not recorded is never billed. Lawyers reconstruct their day from memory at 6:40 pm and reliably remember the long tasks and forget the short ones. Across a firm, even one recovered hour a day is a very large number.

What it does

  • Reads the day from the sources a lawyer already works in and accounts for every activity once.
  • Drafts the entries in 0.1-hour increments with narratives written to the client’s rules.
  • Runs the guard on each draft so a recovered hour does not turn into a rejected one.
  • Waits for approval: nothing is saved to billing until the lawyer approves.
  • Compares remembered time against found time, by matter.

Decisions behind it

  • Approve first. Drafts are never posted; the lawyer approves each entry.
  • Compliance in the same step. The guard’s audit is part of capture, so the narratives come out compliant.
  • Say what it assumes. The $344,300 a year figure on the page is labelled simple arithmetic, not a forecast.

What the recorded run showed

On one lawyer’s day it found 7.3 hours against the 4.1 hours the lawyer would have entered, drafted 15 entries and kept $3,632 payable after the audit. Every activity is accounted for once, and no entry bills more than its logged minutes.

How it was built

Built with Claude Code as a page that calls Claude for the analysis. I set the idea and the test; Claude wrote the page and prompts, and a script recorded the run shown here.

items.title: Party Finder
items.lede: No conflict hides in the paperwork. It reads the complaint, deal documents or engagement request, builds the complete list of names to search, and ties each name to the sentence it came from. The list goes into the firm’s conflicts system, which stays the system of record.
items.body_html:
Try the demoSaved runs on this site; live analysis runs inside Claude

The problem

A conflicts search is only as good as the list of names put into it, and the list comes from an intake form with a few names. The parties that create conflicts are usually in the paperwork: a former name, a parent, an insurer, a co-defendant, a trustee.

What it does

  • Reads the documents and builds a party register with each party’s role, side and relationship.
  • Finds what an intake form misses: former names, parents, affiliates, insurers, counsel, and officers.
  • Explains who is really adverse and why a name matters, ranked by priority.
  • Quotes the source sentence for every name, checked word for word in the page.
  • Exports one row per search name for the firm’s conflicts system.

Decisions behind it

  • Feeds the system, does not replace it. The conflicts system stays the system of record; this fills its input.
  • Every name is traceable. A name with no verified quote does not make the list.
  • An analyst decides. It never clears or declines a matter.

What the recorded run showed

The litigation matter produced 28 parties against 3 on the intake form, and an M&A deal produced 33 against 3. All 61 supporting quotes were found word for word in the documents.

How it was built

Built with Claude Code as a page that calls Claude for the analysis. It grows out of the Conflion conflicts work.

items.title: Matter Desk
items.lede: One desk for the first read of a new matter in five practice areas: M&A diligence, an insurance tender, a PAGA notice, a lease abstract and a health care BAA. It reads the documents, says what a rushed review would miss, dates every deadline and drafts the first letter or email, with every quote checked against the source.
items.body_html:
Try the demoSaved runs on this site; live analysis runs inside Claude

The problem

The first read of a new matter is where things get missed: a consent buried in a customer contract, a notice period that has already run, an amendment that quietly moved a deadline. Each practice group has its own checklist, and a rushed reviewer works from memory.

What it does

  • Five workflows, each driven by a written practice checklist: deal diligence, tender and coverage, PAGA notice intake, lease abstract and dates, and BAA review against a playbook.
  • Bottom line first, then the catches ranked critical, high or medium, each with a next step.
  • Critical dates with the clause and the arithmetic behind each one.
  • The working document for the practice: a consents tracker, a coverage chart, a PAGA issue table, a lease abstract or a clause-by-clause BAA comparison, plus a first draft such as a tender letter or litigation hold.
  • What to ask the client for, and a sign-off checklist for the lawyer.

Decisions behind it

  • Quotes are checked by code. Every quote is matched against the source text in the page, and one that cannot be found is flagged in red.
  • Gaps are marked, not guessed. Open points are labeled for the attorney to confirm.
  • A lawyer decides. Claude drafts; nothing is final until the sign-off checklist is worked through.

What the saved runs show

Each workflow opens on a saved run of a demo matter. Across the five, all 66 quotes were found in the source documents. In the deal workflow, it catches that the largest customer contract treats a change of control as an assignment needing consent, which the seller’s schedules list as needing none.

How it was built

Built with Claude as a page that calls Claude for the analysis. Pasting in a new matter and asking questions of the documents work when the page is opened inside Claude.

items.title: Firm Facts
items.lede: Before a firm can ask an AI agent about its own business, its data needs to be in a shape the agent can query safely. Firm Facts is that layer: one database answering the questions each department actually asks, built over a fully fictional law firm.
items.body_html:

What it answers

  • Finance: "Where are we losing money?" as a realization waterfall by year, practice group and partner, from standard value through write-downs and discounts to cash collected. Plus aged unbilled work and unpaid invoices.
  • Business development: which clients use only one or two practice groups and should hear about the rest.
  • HR: utilization by timekeeper, and who feeds work to whom.
  • Trust accounting: a monthly Rule 1.15 three-way reconciliation with its exceptions.
  • Risk and the general counsel: exposure by severity, plus a one-call client briefing and each client's billing rules.

Built to be safe by default

Thornwood Garza LLP does not exist. Its database was generated with clients, matters, billing, a trust ledger, a docket and documents. The few matters drawn from public court records were stripped out entirely, and a test checks that none come back. Raw tables stay hidden, only read-only views are exposed, and the notes say plainly not to load real firm data without adding sign-in first. A web app and a Microsoft Copilot Studio agent are meant to sit on top of this contract.

How it was built

Built with Claude Code on Supabase (Postgres), with a reproducible seed and a test suite against the database and its REST API. I chose the department questions and the safety rules.

items.title: Name-match bake-off
items.lede: A conflicts check lives or dies on name matching: miss "Wm. Hartley Mfg." when you searched "William Hartley Manufacturing" and a conflict gets through. This benchmark put Conflion's search against seven standard Python methods, from exact match to embeddings, on 300 scenarios.
items.body_html:
Benchmark write-up

Scenarios
300
Hand-written hard cases, held out
48
Methods compared
8
Held-out recall, Conflion
100%
Held-out recall, best Python blend
89.5%

How it was run

  • Two layers: pure name matching, and the full conflicts check, which also has to follow parents, subsidiaries and former names.
  • Fair tuning: every Python method's threshold was tuned on the 252 generated scenarios only. The 48 hand-written hard cases were the test.
  • Strict scoring: namesakes count as false hits, and recall is the number that matters, because a false hit costs an analyst seconds and a miss can let a conflict through.

Catching our own leak

The first run flattered the best Python blend: 97.4% held-out recall. On review, a few rules in its nickname and abbreviation tables ("bill", "mfg", some foreign company suffixes) fired only on the held-out cases, so the test was partly training data. We removed them, reported the clean 89.5% as the main result, kept the contaminated figures alongside, and added a test that fails if any rule fires only on held-out names. The honest caveat stays in the write-up: the scenarios are Conflion's own benchmark.

How it was built

Built with Claude Code as a reproducible Python project with a notebook walk-through and a plain-English explainer. I asked for the comparison and pushed on whether the held-out test was really held out.

items.title: The Deal Desk
items.lede: A daily desk for an M&A law class: the year's live deals, merger-arbitrage spreads and rates, the news that moved them, and a reference to the law behind each one.

What it is

A daily M&A desk built for Katrina's law-school M&A class. It follows the year's live deals, from signing through regulatory review to close, and ties each one back to the law a student is tested on.

What's on it

  • Markets: merger-arbitrage spreads, the 10-year Treasury yield, and each stock deal's offer value against the target's price.
  • Deals and developments: a tracker by stage, deal sizes, and the news that moved each one.
  • Desk reference: deal structures, Delaware standards of review, deal protections, merger agreement terms, approvals, EDGAR filings, cases to know, and practice questions written from live deals.
How it was built

Built with Claude. A small script pulls daily closes for the deal parties and the Treasury yield each morning, and the same page runs as a claude.ai dashboard and as the public site on Cloudflare. I chose the deals and the reference topics with the class in mind.

items.title: Synthesis
items.lede: An M&A workbench for the buy side of one deal. It checks the seller’s disclosure schedules against the reps and the contracts, explains every change in the seller’s markup and proposes a middle position, checks cross-references and defined terms in code, and builds the closing checklist from the agreement.
items.body_html:
Try the demoSaved runs on this site; live analysis runs inside Claude

The problem

Deal lawyers check the same things by hand against a deadline: whether the schedules match the reps and the contracts, what the other side’s markup quietly changed, whether cross-references still point anywhere, and what has to be signed at closing. Each is a separate pass, often done at the last minute.

What it does

  • Deal room: decisions for the deal partner and the next dates, with days to closing and to the outside date.
  • Schedules: each rep set against what the schedule says and what the documents show.
  • Diligence: red flags, each with a checked citation.
  • Turns: every change in the seller’s markup, who it favors, and a proposed middle position.
  • Integrity and Closing: cross-reference and defined-term checks, and a checklist by phase with signature pages.

Decisions behind it

  • Code does what code can. The redline, cross-references, defined terms and date arithmetic are computed in the page, not by the model.
  • Quotes are checked word for word against the deal documents, and anything not found is flagged.
  • Grounded in the work. The page cites what deal lawyers have said in public about each task.

What the saved runs show

On the demo deal, the saved runs find 7 reps the schedules don’t match, 7 major issues in the seller’s markup and 11 of 20 closing items at risk, and the code finds 4 drafting errors. All 37 quotes in the markup analysis were found word for word in the documents.

How it was built

Built with Claude as a page that calls Claude for the analysis. It uses the same deal as Matter Desk’s diligence workflow.

items.title: Case Wins Debrief
items.lede: Reads a firm’s case wins for what slowed them down or left value on the table, groups the lessons into patterns, and pairs each pattern with a working Claude tool.
items.body_html:
Try the demoSaved runs on this site; live analysis runs inside Claude

The problem

Firms announce a win and move on. The lessons in it, such as a legal question that waited years for a motion, a notice that nearly sank a claim, or a fee award never claimed, rarely get collected, so the next team repeats the delay.

What it does

  • Times the wins from the first dated event to the result.
  • Finds patterns across the wins, each tied to the matters behind it.
  • Asks the trial team a question for every win, rather than passing judgment.
  • Four tools, each with a saved run: Day-One Test ranks issues that could end a case early; Notice Monitor checks an event log against a contract’s notice clause; Fee Recovery Builder sorts time entries for a fee motion; Win to Story turns a ruling into a release, an alert angle and a matter-experience entry.

Decisions behind it

  • Questions, not findings. Each "could have gone better" point is something to ask the team.
  • Arithmetic stays in code. The fee tool totals the lodestar in the page.
  • One tool per lesson. Every pattern ends with something a lawyer can run on the next matter.

What the demo shows

Twelve wins produce five patterns: cases won on law that took years, contract wins that turned on notice paperwork, fee-shifting wins that need a clean fee record, wins that came only after a setback, and wins nobody wrote up for clients.

How it was built

Built with Claude as a page that calls Claude for each tool.

items.title: Marketing Studio
items.lede: Drafts law-firm marketing in the firm’s voice, from attorney bios and practice pages to case results, hire announcements and event invites. It then checks every word against the source and the attorney advertising rules of California, New York, Texas, Florida or the ABA Model Rules before anyone publishes it.
items.body_html:
Open Marketing Studio in ClaudeHosted in Claude; example runs and the rule check work right away, and live drafting uses your own Claude account

The problem

Law-firm marketing is drafted from scattered notes and checked late. The risks are specific, and they change from state to state: a "specialist" or superlative claim the rules restrict, a client named without consent, a result with no disclaimer, a missing "Attorney Advertising" label, an ad that had to be filed with the bar first, or a fact nobody can source.

What it does

  • Compliance check: paste any bio, page, ad, post or email. Problems are marked as you type, then Claude reviews it and suggests a rewrite.
  • Eight drafting flows: attorney bio, practice page, client alert, case result, lateral hire, event invite, RFP response and award submission.
  • Five rule sets: California, New York, Texas, Florida and the ABA Model Rules, each flag citing the rule it breaks.
  • Flags on the words: every issue is highlighted where it appears, with a one-click fix by Claude.
  • Sign-off: a checklist and an approval record to keep with the published piece.

Decisions behind it

  • Two checks, not one. A fixed rule check runs in the browser and never misses a banned word or a missing disclaimer. Claude handles the judgment calls.
  • Only facts from the source. Anything missing becomes a marked placeholder, never an invented client, result or referee.
  • Rules read from the source. Each rule set names the text it was checked against, and says so when it is behind.
  • An attorney approves. Nothing is marked ready until the responsible attorney signs off.

What the example runs show

Every flow opens on an example run under California rules. Switch the state and the same drafts are checked again: New York adds the "Attorney Advertising" label and its required results disclaimer, and Texas and Florida add bar filing reminders.

How it was built

Built with Claude as a page hosted in Claude that calls Claude to draft and then to review, with the rule sets checked against each state's published rules.

items.title: RSC Tool
items.lede: Two tools for a small remodeling business: an operations app that runs entirely on one Mac, reads the business inbox with a local AI model and never touches the books without the owner's approval, and a phone-first job tracker that shows what each job really earns once crew hours are counted.
items.body_html:
Click through the demoThe demo is the real app's pages filled with made-up jobs; saving and AI are switched off.

The problem

Jobs, phased payments and expenses lived in a spreadsheet. Receipts, client payments and new leads arrived by email. Estimates, contracts and change orders were written by hand, and nobody could say what a job had cost in labor until it was over.

The constraints shaped everything. The owner is not a programmer, client data had to stay on his computer, and nothing could reach the books or a client without his say.

What it does

Inbox to books

Every 30 minutes a local model reads the inbox read-only and returns a fixed JSON shape at temperature 0. Plain code then matches each receipt, payment or lead to a job: a job ID in the email first, then a unique street address, then a unique client surname. If two jobs fit, it asks.

Labor cost per job

Labor per crew-hour is computed from the estimate's own crew and duration lines, with part-timers counted as half. It warns below the floor rate, compares spend with the estimate's budget, and switches to logged hours once they pass the guess.

Money that adds up

Job IDs, payment IDs and change-order IDs follow one scheme and double as invoice numbers. Payment schedules are generated by rule and tested to the cent. A change order signed with a finger on a phone updates the contract and schedule together.

Hands-free input

Any big text box takes speech through a local Whisper model of about 150 MB. Receipt photos and insurance certificates are read by a local vision model, with the job picked by the same rules as email.

Runs itself

A double-click installer needs no admin password, sizes the models to the Mac's memory, and sets up five background jobs: the app, the mail check, a Monday report, a 6 AM crew sheet and the model server. Daily backups keep 30 copies, and a doctor command checks everything.

Built from research

A market study of the local remodeling trade set the pricing checks: industry margins imply a 43% materials markup rather than 20%, and the crew-hour floor comes from local wage and billing data.

Since the first version

  • Never lost. A five-stage tracker on every job, a glowing next step, and a Next task button.
  • One-click Send. The estimate goes to the client as a PDF from the owner's own Gmail, only when he presses Send.
  • Every attachment read. Each PDF or photo in an email becomes its own item to review.
  • A downloadable Mac app, built and released automatically when the version changes.

In review now: a pricing check before an estimate goes out, a rough range and site-visit questions from a lead's photos, Google review requests, a weekly scorecard of leads and wins, and instant follow-up for website leads.

Decisions behind it

  • The model drafts, code decides. Prices, totals, dates, IDs and job matching are computed in code. If a model's draft drops a required fact, the app falls back to a plain template.
  • Fewer fields. A sentence like "Home Depot 109.91 studs for Smith" fills in an expense. Every page keeps a by-hand form for when the model is off.
  • Nothing sent for him. Emails open in his mail app to read and send. Reminders never mention fees or lawyers.
  • Readable by design. The redesign cut 14 tabs to 5 groups, set text at 18px with nothing under 15px, and made every control at least 48px tall.

Where it goes next

A productizing plan finds about 70% of the app is generic, with the owner-specific parts being configuration rather than architecture. The plan is to treat this business as customer number one, then offer done-for-you setups to three to five local remodelers, with a pilot kit and sales sheet ready.

Part two: the crew job tracker

The second tool answers one question the owner's spreadsheet could not: after materials, subcontractors and crew time, how much does a job actually leave? Hours were invisible, so every job looked more profitable than it was. The tracker puts crew time on the books as money.

Two buttons, every day

Today opens with Log hours and Log a cost, because that two-minute habit is what the whole system depends on. Everything else sits below it: what needs a decision, the week's schedule and the job board.

Money left, live

Set the crew's cost per hour once, and every job shows contract minus materials and subcontractors minus labor. Setup leads with the pricing floor: overhead per hour, break-even and the minimum billable rate.

Six screens, built for a phone

Today, Jobs, a job (work, money and history tabs), Money across all jobs, Archive and Setup, with a bottom tab bar on phones. The first version had no navigation at all below 680px, so a crew member on a phone could not get around.

Change orders and invoices

A change order does not move the contract until the customer approves it, and an approved one can be voided, which reverses it out of the total. Invoices flag when they are past due, and a queue lists costs with no receipt.

Nothing is ever lost

Every removal is reversible and goes to an archive that shows who removed it and why. Deleting a job hides it as a unit and restoring brings back everything attached. Settled records, such as a paid invoice, refuse to delete without an explicit acknowledgement.

Built for four people

The owner plus up to four crew. The first version had six roles with server-side rules, which was too much for a team that size, so the lightweight version trims permissions to roughly viewer, editor and owner.

Two versions, on purpose

  • A full web app. About 6,300 lines across 24 files, with a database, six roles and backups with checksums. Roughly half was inherited from the ChatGPT and Codex first draft; the lifecycle system, query layer, all six screens and the design system are the Claude Code rewrite. It runs on the owner's computer.
  • A shareable version on Claude's artifact pages. Built to be shared with a link. It stores data in the page's shared store and falls back to the phone's own storage if sharing is not available.

What testing caught

  • A migration that would have hidden every job. The generated database migration filled a status column with the literal text of its own name, so no job matched "active" and all of them vanished from every screen. It was reproduced against a rebuilt copy of the live database and patched by hand.
  • No mobile viewport tag. The artifact laid out at desktop width and shrank to unreadable on a real phone. It looked fine on a laptop.
  • Two people logging at once. Each person writes only their own document per job, so two crew members cannot overwrite each other. A second phone's entry updated the first live in testing.
How it was built

Both tools were built with AI. The Mac operations app was built in Claude Code from the owner's real estimates, contract terms and tracker. Claude wrote the code and tests within rules I set. The repo also carries a guide written for the next Claude session on the owner's Mac. It sets out how to explain changes in plain words, back up before any change, keep database migrations additive, test on a copy, and never edit contract text without review.

items.lede: The business's public website, with a blog of plain-spoken repair and remodeling guides for local homeowners. It lives in the same repo as the app, and every change goes through a pull request with its own preview link. Merging is what makes it live.
items.body_html:
Visit rscrafters.comRead the blog

What's on it

Pages for the work that pays

Service pages for kitchens, bathrooms, decks and stairs, restoration and built-ins, and outdoor work, ordered by the jobs the business most wants. Town pages for the surrounding area help it show up in local search.

A blog written to a brief

Each post comes from a keyword plan and a writing brief: plain words, the builder's voice, local detail. The brief bans prices, license and insurance claims, invented testimonials and any claim of past work the business hasn't done.

Safe at Home

A page for aging-in-place work, built from research into local demand and funding programs. It invites a home safety visit and is careful not to claim experience the business doesn't have yet.

A quote form that feeds the app

The quote form asks for as little as possible. I'm wiring it into the office app, where each request becomes a new lead card waiting for the owner's OK.

Checks that block bad pages

The build fails on broken links and on banned wording, so a post that slips in a price or an unconfirmed claim can't go live.

Found by search engines

A sitemap and robots file are built with every page, and the site is verified in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.

How it goes live

  • One source. The site's only source is a folder in the app's repo. Nothing gets dragged, dropped or uploaded by hand.
  • Previews on every change. A GitHub Action builds and checks each pull request and posts a preview link, so the owner can see a change before it's live.
  • Merge to publish. On merge, the Action uploads the build to Cloudflare Pages and then checks that the live domain is serving it.
  • Public means public. Draft notes and placeholders stay out of the live pages. Open questions are kept in the project's notes instead.

Built for the owner to change

The site folder has its own guide for the next AI session on the owner's computer: explain changes in plain words, edit on a branch, run the build, share the preview, and never publish any other way. That lets the owner ask for a change in a sentence without learning Git.

How it was built

Built with Claude, first as a draft site I could share and review, then moved into the repo with Claude Code once the domain was live. Claude wrote the pages, the posts (from my brief and the business's real projects), the build and check scripts, and the deploy Action.

Claymation

Real 3D clay in Blender, rendered on cloud CPUs. Plasticine materials carry fingerprint and smudge texture and a slight frame-to-frame "boil", and the animation runs on twos like stop motion. Long renders are split by frame range across several AI sessions working in parallel, then joined.

Rules that keep it cheap and safe

  • Preview before render. Every new ad starts as an HTML preview or storyboard. Nothing is rendered until it is approved, which saves hours of wasted renders.
  • Modular end cards. Business name, phone, web address and tagline live in one brand file. The end card is its own segment, rendered separately and joined to the body, so a contact change re-renders only the card.
  • Real sound, never synthesized. Effects are free-licence recordings, mixed to one loudness so music fits on top.
  • Honest copy. No prices, no claims of jobs the business hasn't done, and no phone number in captions, where scrapers collect them.

One place to review them

Every ad set, in every style, sits in one private library page with its status: preview, rendered, scheduled or posted. That's where new sets are reviewed and pick what goes out next.

items.lede: Finished ads post themselves to the business's TikTok on a schedule. Nobody uploads a video by hand, the business site never hosts them, and a weekly task keeps the queue full until every ad has gone out.

How a video gets posted

  1. RenderAn approved ad is rendered with its end card and gets a caption from a captions file, with local hashtags and no phone number.
  2. HostThe MP4 is pushed to a public GitHub repo made only for videos, so it has a stable public address.
  3. QueueClaude schedules the post through Buffer's connector at set times in New York time, with TikTok's AI-generated label turned on.
  4. RefillEvery Friday afternoon a scheduled task queues the next week's posts and records each one, so nothing posts twice.
  5. PublishAt post time Buffer fetches the video from the host and publishes it to @rscrafters.

Decisions behind it

  • Buffer, not TikTok's own API. TikTok only lets unaudited apps post privately, so a free Buffer plan does the public posting instead. Its free tier caps the queue at ten posts, which is why the weekly refill exists.
  • A repo as the video host. Buffer copies a video only when it posts, so the file has to stay up until then. A public repo is free, simple to push to from anywhere, and keeps the videos off the business's own website.
  • Launch, then a steady pace. The clay ads launched with a three-a-day burst over three days, then settled at about five a week.

What stays human

Following, commenting and replying are done by hand. TikTok quietly undoes automated follows, and real replies from the business matter more than volume. Profile changes behind TikTok's bot check also need a person to press Save.

How it was built

Built with Claude, using Buffer's MCP connector to schedule posts and a Claude scheduled task for the weekly refill. Claude also set up the TikTok profile and wrote the captions and the growth plan.

items.title: Fieldwork
items.lede: An evidence-first Mac app for data-licensing deal scouts. It researches established businesses from public sources, checks them against buyer requirements, prepares outreach for human approval, collects owner consent and keeps a commission ledger. It prepares research and drafts, and a person makes every outreach, consent and introduction decision.
items.body_html:
Screenshots below, from the app's built-in demo

The problem

AI labs and data brokers pay referral fees for introductions to established businesses that hold years of operating records. A business listing is only the start: someone still has to establish which records exist, who controls them, whether a buyer wants them, whether the owner wants an introduction, and how referral credit is recorded. Treating a company score as a qualified deal hides the work that matters. Fieldwork aims to deliver a small queue of opportunities, each with its sources and an explicit list of what still blocks an introduction.

What it does today

  • Research: a background job queue reads each company's public pages and records every claim with its source and a confidence label. A discovery queue proposes new businesses from public directories for review, flagging likely duplicates.
  • Buyer requirements: each buyer program's criteria and the referral agreement are recorded separately, with review dates, so expired terms stop counting.
  • Prospect briefs: what is known, what still needs proof, likely record categories, and a fit hypothesis for each buyer naming the missing facts.
  • Outreach preparation: drafts for sourced contacts, approved by a person before any campaign can send.
  • Owner intake, deals and commissions: a single-use owner questionnaire with buyer-specific consent, a deal register, and an append-only ledger of invoices and payments.

Accountable automation

Readiness is recomputed, never stored

An opportunity is "ready for introduction review" only while every check passes: current buyer terms and mandate, verified facts, minimum size and record history, owner consent for that buyer, no suppression, and no competing introduction. Change any of them and it drops back with the reason listed.

Reviews bound to a fingerprint

The final human review signs a hash of the company record, the buyer's requirements, the owner's answers and the fact reviews. If any of those changes afterwards, the review no longer counts and the packet has to be looked at again.

Approval of exact messages

Campaign approval is bound to the exact text and recipients and expires. Sending also needs mail credentials, a separate delivery switch, daily limits and an unsuppressed contact. A send that crashes midway becomes "needs reconciliation" rather than being retried, so it can't double-send.

Durable background work

Research jobs live in the database with retries and backoff, and permanent failures are blocked with the reason shown. Daily usage limits cap research and paid search, which starts off.

A careful crawler

It obeys robots.txt, resolves each hostname first and refuses private or local network addresses. An optional local model may read page text, but its output is stored as a research hypothesis, never as a fact.

Money that adds up

The commission ledger only adds entries, and each one has a unique request key so a retried click can't double-count. Expected revenue shows as "Unknown" rather than a guess.

In use on my Mac

Fieldwork runs on my own Mac with research switched on. Its workspace holds 92 company research records, 109 contact records, 109 prepared outreach drafts and 361 sourced evidence rows, with a buyer referral agreement confirmed and on file.

Built as a desktop product

  • Native Mac app: a Swift, AppKit and WebKit window around a bundled Python runtime, so it needs no Python install. Apple Silicon, macOS 14 or later, signed locally but not notarized by Apple.
  • Data kept separate: the workspace lives outside the app, with automatic backups, and a one-time migration moved the original database across with its records intact.
  • Standard-library Python and SQLite with a plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript interface. Customer builds ship without any data, and a read-only fictional demo can be explored safely.
  • Tests: 89 backend and workflow tests and 3 desktop tests (startup without system Python, migration that preserves records, rejection of a corrupt database).
How it was built

Built with ChatGPT and Codex, from my product direction, workflow design and testing. An optional local model, run through Ollama, can read public page text and suggest what a business does; the app labels that output an unverified hypothesis.

items.title: Permit Postcards
items.lede: When a homeowner pulls a permit for a kitchen remodel, the contractor on the permit already has the job. The countertop shop, the tile setter and the window installer who come next do not know about it yet. Permit Postcards turns fresh building permits from twelve California permit feeds into leads for those next trades, and lets a contractor work them on a map.
items.body_html:
Open Permit PostcardsPublic permit records. Your statuses and notes save in your own browser only

The problem

Building permits are public, and they are the earliest reliable sign that a home project is about to need a lot of trades. But the feeds are raw: thousands of rows a week in each city's own format, with work descriptions like "5 bathroom(s). Bathroom remodel... Kitchen remodel" and no contact details. A small contractor has no way to watch them, and the trade that pulled the permit is the one company that does not need the lead.

What it does

  • Reads the permits: a pipeline pulls the last 45 days from each city or county source and sorts every permit into project kinds (kitchen, bath, roof, pool, ADU, addition, new home, solar, demolition and more) with editable keyword rules and a test file of real-looking cases.
  • Finds the next trades: each kind maps to the trades that follow it. A kitchen remodel goes to countertops, cabinets, appliances and flooring; a pool goes to fencing and landscaping.
  • Says when to call: each trade enters a project at a different stage, so every lead shows the best time to reach out, from "now" to "probably already done".
  • Scores the lead: Hot, Warm or Cool, from points a contractor can read: timing, project value, how well the project fits the trade, and the neighborhood's home values and owner-occupancy.
  • Works as a CRM: each lead moves from New to Contacted, Quoting, Won or Lost, with follow-up dates, notes and a printable postcard as one action on the lead.

How it changed

It started as a postcard generator. Working with it, I decided the product is not the postcard but the map as a CRM: new permits arrive as leads already filtered to your trade, and a postcard is one thing you can do with a lead. The design rule I set was "way simpler and easier, with nested complexity". A lead-intelligence pass then added timing and scoring, and a final redesign took it from a prototype look to a calm, dense tool a contractor would pay for monthly: one sans typeface, a sidebar list with a detail panel, keyboard search and a single safety-orange accent.

Keeping it current

One command refreshes everything: it pulls the newest permits from every source, redraws the US Census outline basemap around wherever the permits now are, runs the classifier tests and stops if any fail, then rebuilds the page. If a city's feed is down, the run says so and keeps the rest.

How it was built

Built with Claude Code from specs I wrote for each stage: the prototype, the CRM, the lead intelligence and the professional redesign. The pipeline is plain Python and the app is plain HTML and JavaScript with Leaflet. I chose the idea, the trades and their timing, and made the product calls along the way.

What it does

The six that repeat

  • Speed-to-lead reply: thank them within a minute, ask two qualifying questions, offer a booking link.
  • Quote follow-up: a nudge on day two, a check-in on day five and a close-the-loop on day ten.

Rules they all follow

  • A customer’s reply stops everything and puts the conversation in front of the owner.
  • Quiet hours, a log of who approved what and when, and a pause button for any single automation.
How it was built

The sample screens were built with Claude from workflows I mapped by hand. The same six are what Front Office runs as a product, and the same pattern (draft, wait for approval, stop when the customer answers) is what the Northfield tools above do for a brokerage.

items.title: Thrifty Vows
items.lede: A budget-first wedding planner for iPhone and Mac that plans the whole day around one number: what the couple can actually afford. It went from product plan to a working app, then through a full visual redesign, "Blush & Petal", with a custom icon, dark mode and a native Mac build.
items.body_html:
Watch the walkthrough and try the budget toolsScreenshots below come from the app's built-in sample wedding

The problem

The big wedding apps, The Knot, Zola and WeddingWire, earn money by selling couples' details to vendors and pushing registries, so their design nudges spending up. The couples who most need help are those with under about $15,000 to spend (the US average is around $33,000), usually paying for it themselves and planning without a planner.

Thrifty Vows earns money only from the couple, so it can be honest about spending less. The plan is a free core app and a one-time Pro unlock for sync, sharing, exports and widgets, with no subscription.

What it does

  • Budget: a total split into 13 categories by a recommended budget-wedding allocation, with estimate, final cost, amount paid and due date on every expense.
  • The guest-count lever: a calculator separates fixed costs from the ones that grow with each guest, and shows in dollars what adding or cutting people does.
  • Guests and RSVPs: sides, A and B lists, plus-ones, meals and households, swipe to RSVP, and CSV export.
  • Checklist: tasks dated backwards from the wedding and grouped by phase. Move the date and the open tasks move with it.
  • Vendors, seating and DIY: quotes compared side by side, with a booking written straight into the budget; tables with capacity warnings; and DIY projects that weigh making against buying.
  • Savings tips: concrete tips, each with a typical saving, that add to a running total on the home screen.

Decisions behind it

Savings first, not spend first

The home screen leads with money saved and cost per guest, where the big wedding apps lead with vendors and inspiration.

Useful in the first minute

A sample wedding loads on first launch, so there is something to explore before typing anything. One switch in Settings clears it.

Opinionated defaults

The budget split, checklist and tips are pre-filled for a budget wedding. Food and venue get the largest shares, and a contingency line is kept on purpose.

Private by design

No account, no backend and no third-party code. Everything is stored on the device and works offline; iCloud sync is planned as part of Pro.

Built to grow

SwiftUI and SwiftData with simple models, so sync, sharing and widgets can be added without restructuring.

Gentle and personal

Heart-shaped checkboxes, a little confetti and haptics when a task is done, and copy such as "Budget is looking lovely" instead of spreadsheet language.

The 2.0 redesign

Version 1 worked but looked like stock iOS. Version 2.0, "Blush & Petal", was designed first as a mockup and then built into the app: rose for actions, blush cream behind everything, sage for money saved and champagne for neutral highlights, with serif headings over rounded body text. It added a custom icon of interlocking rings, a dark mode with its own plum palette, and a native Mac version of the same app.

Where it goes next

  • 1.1: iCloud sync and partner sharing, contacts import, PDF export and a countdown widget.
  • 1.2: a shareable RSVP link, a day-of timeline and payment reminders.
  • Later: anonymous price benchmarks by city, and swap suggestions such as a brunch reception instead of dinner.

Measures of success

Couples set a budget and add at least ten guests in their first week, the median saving logged per couple, Pro conversion, and an App Store rating of 4.7 or better.

How it was built

Built with Claude, from a one-line brief: an industry-leading app for planning a cheap wedding. Claude wrote the product plan, the SwiftUI code, the 2.0 design mockup and the redesign, then built and ran the app on my Mac and took the screenshots. I set the direction and reviewed each round.

The song workflow

The songs are written with Suno, and the process is a written system: concept, style, structure, meter, hook, verses, then a rhyme audit and a length audit before anything is generated. After generating, the song is diagnosed before it is rewritten. The full workflow runs to 17 steps; these are the ideas that matter most.

Start with the premise

Name the core concept, point of view, emotional tone and the central joke or tension, and brainstorm scenes and images before any lyric. Comedy works best when the singer treats an absurd premise completely seriously. The joke is never explained; it comes out of the character's logic.

A separate style prompt

Genre, BPM, drum feel, bass, harmony, instruments, vocal register and timbre, texture, space and mood, in under about 1,000 characters. The instrumental should sound like a real record first: future garage, neo-soul, dub, dancehall, vintage calypso, synth-funk, jazz-funk. Funny lyrics don't need funny production, and the contrast is often what makes them funny.

Lock structure, then meter

Sections are decided before writing, and equivalent sections get equivalent line counts (8, 12 or 16, never a verse that runs long because it has more jokes). A syllable pattern is set per section, such as 8/8/8/8 or 7/10/7/10, with an even stricter meter in the chorus because the music model needs a predictable shape.

The hook is designed on its own

A short repeated phrase of three to five syllables with a repeated grammatical construction and simple words: "Kitty computer", "No teef, big life". The chorus gets its own identity instead of summarising the verses.

Verses are distinct scenes

Concrete images, physical detail and character-specific logic. When several characters sing, each has a different worldview, vocabulary and kind of joke, and no two are interchangeable.

Rhyme with rules

End, internal, multisyllabic and slant rhyme, with several rhyme points inside a line when it comes naturally. No word rhymed with itself, no lazy pseudo-rhymes such as side and outside, and no bent syntax to force a rhyme. Sound beats spelling.

Written to be sung

Where do the stresses fall, can the singer breathe, are the vowels good for held notes, and does each line have a rhythmic shape like its neighbour? A lyric can look clever on paper and still generate badly if the meter is unstable.

Realistic runtime, musical endings

The target is about 3:15 to 3:30. If a lyric is too long, cut the weaker jokes and shorten the bridge rather than rush the model. Endings are a refrain, a stripped hook, a harmony stack or an instrumental fade, not a spoken skit.

Arrangements that evolve

Dropouts, countermelodies, filtered passages, bass breaks, drum changes, vocal stacks, dub-delay throws, sparse bridges and a bigger final chorus, so the track develops instead of looping. Vocals are described precisely, for example a high, clear, intimate lead with airy falsetto edges, close-mic phrasing, whispered doubles and soft stacked harmonies.

Quality control before output

Fifteen checks run on every lyric: equal line counts in matching verses, the intended syllable pattern, a consistent chorus meter, a short memorable hook, no self-rhymes or lazy rhymes, internal and multisyllabic rhyme present, no line much denser than its neighbours, a lyric that scans out loud, distinct verses, a realistic runtime, a joke that is embodied rather than explained, a musical ending, and a production prompt that sounds like a real record. The output is always two copyable blocks, a style prompt and the lyrics, with no long explanations.

Diagnose before rewriting

  • Confused melody: check syllable count and line length.
  • Weak chorus: simplify it and repeat more.
  • Rushed verses: cut density or cut lines.
  • Feels childish: make the production more serious.
  • Forced jokes: go back to character perspective and concrete detail.
  • Weak rhymes: rewrite the rhyme structure instead of patching words.

Concept, style, structure, meter, hook, verses, rhyme audit, length audit, generate, diagnose, revise.

Cat Music Video Studio

A toolkit that connects a recorded song to a timed storyboard and animated character performances. Turning a finished song into a video means coordinating several timelines at once: the recording, the lyrics, the characters' performances and the visual story. Written lyrics don't capture how a singer actually delivers them, and repeated hooks, held vowels, pauses, ad-libs and changed pronunciations all make synchronisation hard. I directed the AI-assisted build of the tool that solves it.

An interactive review tool

One browser workspace holds the song, the isolated vocal, the lyrics and the storyboard. Words and lines are clickable to audition them, master and vocal switch without losing your place, and playback speed slows difficult phrases. A waveform seeks on click, the current word highlights live, and search and section filters move through verses and choruses. Review flags and confidence labels mark uncertain alignment, and a storyboard view ties timed scenes to actions, camera direction, continuity notes and generation prompts.

Audio analysis and alignment

Scripts decode the master and the isolated vocal, measure both, and compare sync at several points. Whisper recognition and reference-conditioned alignment propose word and line timings, and separate analysis of each stem gives evidence to compare them. Targeted passes handle the hard parts: repeated calls, short interjections and closing phrases. The data keeps supplied lyrics, model recognition, candidate timestamps and unresolved events apart, so uncertainty stays visible.

Production data other tools can use

JSON for timing maps, audio metadata, lyrics, scenes and review evidence. CSV for word and line timings, sections, non-lyric intervals, scene plans and review logs. SRT for draft captions. HTML for an interactive review package with the timing data embedded. Together they give audio, shots, captions and animation one shared timeline.

The songs

Fourteen songs so far, all starring my cats, written and generated with the workflow above and collected in one YouTube playlist.

  • Why You Chase Me, Newty?
  • On Mi Turf
  • No Teef, Big Life
  • Mommy Saved Mi
  • Who Puke Pon di Floor?
  • Vet Day Come
  • Mi Nah Like Moving Day
  • Every Lane, Every Road
  • Free Di Claw
  • Shoulda Leave di Treats Alone
  • Please Turn on di Sink
  • Flea Pon Me
  • Kitty Computer
  • Open up the Door

A finished animation

A complete music video built in the browser with p5.js, combining character drawings, environments, timed shots, captions and the original song. Mouth opening follows word timing and vocal amplitude, the mouth closes between timed words, and singing can be switched on or off per shot. Mouth and tongue shapes respond to the resulting value. It has play, seek, restart, mute, caption and fullscreen controls, plus a rendered vertical-video version.

  • "Every Lane, Every Road": a 34-shot animated video, about 3 minutes 33 seconds, exported at 1080 × 1920 and 25 fps.
  • "Why You Run Me Down, Newty?": 627 word records and 44 proposed shots.
  • "Mommy Save Mi": 567 word records and 42 proposed shots.

Built with

Python, Whisper small.en, stable-ts, FFmpeg, NumPy, SciPy, soundfile, JavaScript, HTML and CSS, and p5.js.

My role

I set the creative goals, supplied the songs and characters, directed the AI-assisted build, and shaped the workflow through requirements and feedback. It was built through an iterative ChatGPT and Codex workflow, which wrote the implementation, analysis scripts, production documents and animation code.
