What each specimen gives you

  • A live sample, drawn in the browser rather than shown as a picture.
  • Controls built from the specimen's own settings, so a palette, a seed or a speed can be changed and seen at once.
  • Standalone code that reproduces exactly what is on screen, with a copy button.
  • A permanent accession number, its source and its license, so a specimen can be cited in a brief.

How a page with 1,520 live pieces stays fast

  • Loaded by cabinet: each cabinet's code arrives only when one of its specimens is about to be seen.
  • Mounted near the screen only, a few per frame, and stopped again when scrolled away. Animation also pauses in background tabs.
  • A WebGL budget: browsers keep about 16 live 3D contexts, so the archive holds at most 9 and unloads the ones farthest from the middle of the screen.
  • Sealed styles: every specimen renders in its own shadow root, so no specimen's CSS can leak into another.

Where this site's effects came from

The picture index, the numbers that count up, the paper grain, the shader backdrops, the before-and-after sliders and the reading bar on this page were all chosen from the archive and rebuilt to fit this site's colours and appearance settings.

Specimen Builder: a website from the archive

Describe a business in a sentence, such as a record shop with a listening bar, and the builder lays out a one-page site from the archive's navigation bars, heroes, sections, forms and footers. Then it makes the result look like one site instead of a collage of seven.

What makes it helpful

  • Starts from a brief. Claude picks a starter page of five to eight blocks and says why each fits. Without Claude, a local scorer fills the same slots from the brief's words, so it always works.
  • One theme for the whole site. Fourteen themes built from the archive's own palettes and type pairings, or "from this block" to borrow the look of one you like.
  • Copy for your business. Claude rewrites each block's text for the brief, keeping lengths close, and every line can be edited by hand.
  • Exports one file that rebuilds the page on load, as a normal web page or a page ready to publish on Claude.

The hard part: one site, not a collage

Every specimen arrives with its own fonts, colours and invented brand. The re-skin pass reads every colour in a block, sorts it by tone against that block's own background, and maps it onto the theme's ramp, with strong colours becoming the accent. Fonts follow the theme, and the shop's name replaces each specimen's fake brand in headers and footers. A final pass pushes any text below the AA contrast standard back toward legibility.

Checked on 231 blocks across seven cabinets with no render errors, and on 156 text pairs in three themes with none below AA. The same check on the unthemed page finds failures, so it can fail.

How it was built

Built with Claude Code under my direction. I chose what goes into each cabinet and judged every specimen; Claude wrote the specimens, the catalog, the archive's viewer and the Specimen Builder, and Gemini added two batches of form and section specimens following a written guide. When the first version of the builder produced collages, I said so, and the second version was rebuilt around the theme and re-skin pass.

Built like a jeweler would build it

  • Stones cut to real proportions. The round brilliant uses angles from the top of the grading scale, and every shape's size comes from its standard weight formula, so a 3 ct oval and a 3 ct emerald show their real difference face up.
  • Settings from real jewelry CAD. Prong thickness, head height and the swell of the band under the head were measured from openly licensed casting models and matched.
  • Halos, side stones, pavé bands, split shanks, cathedral arches and twists, each fitted around the chosen center stone rather than placed as a fixed part.
  • A casting file. The ring downloads as an STL at true size, metal alone or with every stone in its seat, which a jeweler's CAD program opens.

Why the stones look real

  • Light is traced through each stone wavelength by wavelength, with each gem's measured refractive index and dispersion. That is where the coloured flashes of fire come from.
  • Four lighting rooms, from a catalogue light tent to store spotlights and candlelight, because a stone only sparkles against light and dark around it.
  • A light performance map shows the stone from above the way a gem lab's ASET scope does, so a badly proportioned stone looks bad here too.
  • Photo mode path-traces the metal for a catalogue-quality still, and video mode records a turntable clip.

Help with the decision, not just the picture

  • What it should cost: a range built from current online retail listings, scaled by the stone's grade, plus the metal's weight in grams worked out from the ring's own volume.
  • Try-on: a hand-tracking model finds the ring finger in a photo or the live camera and sits the ring on it, with a soft shadow on the skin. It all runs on the phone.
  • Compare: pin up to three builds and see them side by side, or copy a short design code to share one.
  • True size shows the ring at its real size on screen.

Ready for a real store

The builder drops into a jeweler's own site. I built four invented jewelry shops around it, each in a different style, where every product photo in the catalogue is rendered from the builder itself, so a store can add a design without a photo shoot. The pitch to a store: a modern site, online booking and a ring builder its customers can play with.

How it was built

I set the bar, a builder that could sit on a real jeweler's site, and reviewed every round against real ring photos; Claude wrote the 3D modelling, the optics, the pricing, try-on and the demo stores, researched openly licensed ring CAD to check its proportions against, and rendered the comparison sheets used to judge each change.

The scenes

The first eight are originals: the lantern, a fog-bound graveyard, a bubbling cauldron over magenta fire, eyes in the dark that follow your cursor, a lightning-lit manor, drifting ghosts, a spider on its web and the catacombs. The next seven are classic horror: the Overlook hallway with its hexagon carpet and the twins, the cursed tape climbing out of the TV, Nosferatu's shadow on the stairs, Frankenstein's laboratory, the Psycho drain dissolving into an eye, the Exorcist streetlamp, and The Birds gathering on the wires.

How it's drawn

Each scene writes a brightness and a colour channel into a grid of character cells, and one renderer turns brightness into characters from a density ramp. Some scenes are simulations, such as the fire, the rain and the flocking birds; the pumpkin is a signed-distance model ray-marched per cell. A blurred copy of the canvas, blended on top, gives the glow.

My role

I set the brief, pushed it well past the obvious, asked for the classic-film set, and chose what stayed. Claude Code wrote the code.

items.title: Aurora Lake
items.lede: Northern lights over a mountain lake, made to be sat with: the light breathes at six breaths a minute, the water ripples where you move, and clicking releases a paper lantern into the sky.
items.body_html:
Open Aurora LakeMove over the water, click to release a lantern, press S for sound

What's in it

  • Aurora curtains that drift and fold, built from layered noise per column.
  • Mountain ridgelines traced in slash and caret characters, snow catching the light.
  • A star field wheeling around the pole, a faint Milky Way and the odd shooting star.
  • A mirror lake that reflects everything, broken by swells and by your ripples.
  • Fireflies, swaying reeds and lanterns, each with its own reflection.

The breathing

The aurora brightens and dims on a ten-second cycle, which is a calm breathing pace, so you can breathe along with it. An optional ambient pad is synthesised live in the browser and swells with the same cycle; there are no audio files.

My role

The brief was to make the most beautiful, entrancing ASCII art I could. I judged each pass and Claude Code built and rebuilt it until the composition held.

items.title: Prism Trip
items.lede: A psychedelic light show in full-colour text with eight modes, from a wormhole and a kaleidoscope to a morphing fractal and living reaction-diffusion patterns. It also runs natively inside AgentForge, my Mac app.
items.body_html:
Open Prism TripKeys 1–8 switch modes; C auto-cycles; F goes fullscreen

The eight modes

  • Wormhole and Hypno spiral, both steered by the cursor.
  • Kaleidoscope, eight mirrors around a blooming centre.
  • Plasma, the classic demoscene colour waves.
  • Fractal, a Julia set whose seed you bend with the cursor.
  • Interference, ripples from moving sources, one following you.
  • Turing, reaction-diffusion growing coral and mazes; drag to seed it.
  • Liquid, noise folded into itself until it flows like oil on water.

In the browser and on the Mac

On the web, each cell picks one of 504 colours (36 hues by 14 brightness levels), and characters are drawn in batches by colour. In AgentForge it is a TRIP tab in ASCII Studio, written in Swift: glyphs are pre-tinted into tiles once, so each frame is a set of memory copies into one image, with a borderless fullscreen view on top.

My role

I asked for a psychedelic version with modes, then for it inside AgentForge. Claude Code wrote both, the browser piece and the Swift port.

items.title: Notre-Dame, turning
items.lede: The cathedral as a real 3D model drawn in characters, turning on a turntable, with day, golden-hour and floodlit-night lighting.
items.body_html:
Open Notre-DameDrag to turn it; pick a time of day

The model

The building is a set of signed-distance shapes: the west front and its towers, the nave and side aisles under a pitched lead roof, the transept, the rounded east end, repeating flying buttresses and the spire. Rose windows, portals and belfry louvres are painted onto the faces where they belong, and the cathedral casts a moving shadow on the plaza.

The light

By day the sun lights each wall in turn as the building rotates. At night floodlights come up from below and the rose windows glow blue and red. The palette blends smoothly through the cycle.

My role

I asked for a cathedral, then rejected the flat façade and asked for 3D. Claude Code built it.

items.title: Empire State, turning
items.lede: The Empire State Building and the Midtown blocks around it, turning in 3D, with the crown lit orange and purple after dark. You can change how the text itself looks.
items.body_html:
Open Empire StateDrag to turn it; set detail, weight and characters

What changes

  • Detail: 40 to 150 rows of characters, from chunky to fine.
  • Weight: light, regular, semibold or bold.
  • Characters: a classic ramp, a dense 70-character ramp, or solid block shading.
  • Time of day: day, golden hour or night, or a slow cycle.

The city

Office windows light up in a random scatter at night, streetlights come on along the avenues, and by day the tower's shadow sweeps across the streets. The antenna is too thin to ray-march, so it's drawn as a line with a depth test against the scene.

My role

I asked for the building and for controls over how the text looks. Claude Code built it.

items.title: Skippy, turning
items.lede: My orange tabby, Skippy, as a 3D model drawn in characters and turning 360° on a loop, modelled from photos down to his sleepy half-lidded eyes.
items.body_html:
Open SkippyDrag to spin him

How he's made

Skippy is built from blended ellipsoids for the body, head, cheeks, muzzle and paws, cones for the ears, and a chain of capsules for the tail. Tabby stripes come from his position on the body, the eyes are painted onto the face with slit pupils, and he blinks every few seconds. I supplied the photos; Claude Code built the model.

items.title: Living Processes
items.lede: A teaching gallery of eight animal and ecosystem processes animated in text, from the Great Migration to metamorphosis, each opening fullscreen with notes on what to watch for.
items.body_html:
Open Living ProcessesClick any plate to open it fullscreen

The plates

  • The Great Migration, month by month between the Serengeti and the Masai Mara.
  • A starling murmuration that ripples when a falcon dives in.
  • Geese in V-formation, taking turns at the front.
  • A salmon run up a waterfall, past a bear, to the spawning gravel.
  • The monarch migration across four generations to Mexico.
  • Lynx and hare populations rising and crashing.
  • Ant trails forming from pheromones.
  • Metamorphosis from egg to butterfly.

For the classroom

Each plate names the stage it's in as it happens ("Aug · crossing the Mara River · crocodiles wait"), gives the real scale behind the compressed time, and pauses with a click so a teacher can talk through a moment. Several plates are simulations rather than scripts: the flock, the ants and the predator–prey cycle all run on simple rules.

My role

I set the subject and the audience, and redirected it from cell biology to animals and ecosystems. Claude Code built it.

items.html:
AI tools and experiments

Small tools that put AI reasoning on display.

items.title: BLACKBOX
items.lede: A flight recorder for AI coding agents. It captures what Claude Code actually did, prompts, tool calls, file edits, failures and subagent handoffs, and lets you replay a session, trace a file change back to the agent that made it, and see how a failure was recovered. Nothing leaves the Mac.
items.body_html:
Take the guided tourScreens from the running Mac app, with synthetic sessions

The problem

AI coding agents now run for long stretches, start subagents and edit dozens of files. When something breaks, the only record is a scrolling transcript. There is no way to see the session as a whole, ask which agent changed a file, or tell what was observed from what someone guessed afterward.

What it does

  • Capture, local only: opt-in hooks and transcript import into a local database, with privacy levels and redaction.
  • Replay on a single timeline, with an inspector that links each event to its cause and result.
  • File forensics, agent topology and a failure observatory that groups repeated failures and reconstructs recovery.
  • A safe installer that shows a line-by-line diff of the Claude settings file and backs it up before changing anything.
How it was built

A native macOS app in SwiftUI over SQLite with full-text search. I wrote the specification package and asked for it to be as sleek as a flight instrument; Claude Code built the app, the hook relay and the synthetic sessions, and ran the builds on my Mac through Remote Control.

items.title: AgentForge
items.lede: A Mac app for running AI agents on models that live on your own computer. You point an agent at a project folder, choose how much it may touch, and approve each change. It also covers chat, chat with your documents and visual agent workflows, all inside a retro terminal look built from text characters.
items.body_html:
Download for MacSigned, notarized and self-updating. Needs Ollama, which the first-run setup installs.

Lines of Swift
10,442
Pages
19
Agent harnesses
3
Automated checks
32
Releases shipped
4
Cloud accounts required
0

What it does

Agents on your own models

A built-in agent lists, reads, searches, writes and edits files and runs commands, using a model running locally through Ollama. Access is chosen per session: read only, ask before each change, or auto-approve edits. Every change is checkpointed and can be undone.

Three harnesses

The same launcher also drives Claude Code and Codex, either on the user's own cloud account or pointed at a local model. Skills and MCP tools plug in, and a timed-out run can be continued, with the agent told which files the last attempt already changed.

Model Lab

Grades each installed model on whether it can drive an agent: does it make real tool calls, how fast does it write, and how long does it take to wake. The agent picker defaults to the best-graded model.

Flows

A drag-and-drop canvas for wiring agents, prompts, routers, human approval gates and shell steps into a workflow, with zoom, fit, a minimap and ten starter templates. One template has an agent edit AgentForge itself, rebuild it and relaunch it.

Library

Chat with your own documents. PDFs, Word files and code are split up and indexed with a local embedding model, and answers cite the passage they came from. Agents can search the library too.

The fun parts

Idea Forge, a slot machine that rolls a project idea; ASCII Studio with effects and 24 animated creatures; Sprite Lab, where a model can draw a sprite from a prompt; a music visualizer; and an Agent Theater where running agents appear as characters.

Making small local models usable as agents

Local models fail as agents in quiet ways. Some write a tool call as text instead of making it, some announce the next step and then stop, and some repeat the same action forever. The harness recovers tool calls written as text, nudges a model that promised an action it did not take, redirects and then stops repeat loops, and frees memory and reloads the model onto the graphics chip before a long run. Model Lab measures which models need this help, so the default is one that does not.

How it was built

Built with Claude Code as a native SwiftUI app with no third-party code apart from the Sparkle updater. Every animation is plain text redrawn by a capped clock, and everything pauses when the window is in the background. Releases are signed with my Apple Developer ID, notarized by Apple and served from a Cloudflare Worker that also hosts the update feed. A feedback button attaches diagnostics and recent crash reports, with personal paths removed.

kickers: Desktop app for Mac, Windows and Linux · Local AI
items.title: AgentForge Rust Edition
items.lede: AgentForge rebuilt in Rust so it runs on Mac, Windows and Linux, reskinned in rusted iron and forge orange. It carries every feature of the Mac app, then adds cloud models, an image studio, a cost tracker, one queue for every approval, and visualizers simulated in Rust that react to whatever the computer is playing.
items.body_html:
Download for Mac, Windows or LinuxSigned and notarized on the Mac; updates itself on Mac and Windows. See also the original Mac app.

What changed from the Mac app

Three operating systems

A Rust backend (Tauri) with a Svelte interface replaces SwiftUI. Agents, file tools, Ollama, MCP servers, document search and hardware readings all run in Rust, so they behave the same on Mac, Windows and Linux. A first-run setup finds Ollama or walks through installing it on each one.

Cloud models and images

Local models stay the default, but chat and agents can also use OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, DeepSeek, Kimi, Mistral, Groq, xAI, OpenRouter or any OpenAI-compatible server. Keys stay in the system keychain, and a notice appears whenever text is about to leave the computer. Image Studio generates and edits pictures, also from chat with /image.

Cost and approvals

Every model call is logged with its tokens and cost: the provider's own figure when it reports one, otherwise tokens times a price I set, and $0 for local models. Every pending approval, from any agent or workflow, lands in one queue where it can be approved or denied.

Visualizers simulated in Rust

Seventeen effects are written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly. Six of them listen: Chladni Plate, Ferrofluid, Forge Hammer, Iron Filings, Murmuration and Molten Pour. A test showed Rust drawing every pixel was far slower than the graphics chip, so these simulate at a low resolution and scale up as crisp pixels, which keeps them smooth and suits the look. Each one doubles as a window background that moves on its own, or reacts to music if you switch that on. The audio can come from the microphone, a file, or the computer's own output, captured natively on all three systems.

How it was built

Built with Claude Code in two days. One session planned the port and gave each feature its own folder in the code, then several builder agents worked in parallel on separate branches while it merged, tested and released them. Features I liked in one edition, like the cost tracker and the approvals queue, went into the Mac app first and were carried over once I had tried them. The interface screenshots here use the app's built-in demo data.

items.title: Argument X-ray
items.lede: Persuasive writing hides its structure. This tool maps a text into its thesis, claims, evidence, unstated assumptions and objections, then flags the weak links so you can see what is actually supported.
items.body_html:
Open Argument X-ray

What it does

  • A clickable map of each text: thesis, reasons, evidence, unstated assumptions, objections and replies. Selecting a box highlights its passage, and selecting a passage selects its box.
  • A verdict with a grade, the weak points ranked by how serious they are, and suggested fixes. Typical findings are false dilemmas, one-off costs passed off as yearly ones, and contract clauses that conflict.
  • A rule-based scan beside it, so you can see what plain pattern matching catches and what takes real reading.
How it was built

Claude Code wrote the page, the sample texts and each analysis. The look is deliberately separate from this portfolio: a dark radiology light box, where the examples are plates and the fixes are recommendations.

items.title: Boardroom of One
items.lede: Ask one AI for advice and you tend to get one balanced, agreeable answer that hides the real disagreement. This tool seats five advisers with fixed temperaments and lets them argue your decision, then vote.
items.body_html:
Open Boardroom of One

How a meeting runs

  • Five temperaments: Skeptic, Optimist, CFO, Future You and Contrarian, each with a different worldview.
  • Openings, cross-examination and a vote on a five-point scale, which you can replay turn by turn around an animated table.
  • The chair's resolution: the crux, the tradeoffs, when to say yes or no, and a first step for this week.
How it was built

Claude Code built the page and wrote the four example debates. It has its own look, an after-hours boardroom with a brass-nameplate table and a chair's resolution sealed in wax, so it reads as a separate product.

items.title: Small-model proof
items.lede: Can a free model that runs on a laptop pull the parties out of a lawsuit as well as Claude? And does training it on industry data make it better? One test on 100 real federal complaints answered both, and the second answer was no.
items.body_html:
Experiment write-up

Federal complaints tested
100
Parties in the answer key
353
Parties found, Claude Sonnet
99.2%
Parties found, 4B model on a laptop
98.9%
Parties found, same model after training
91.5%

The question

Pulling every party out of a new complaint is the first step of a conflicts check, and a missed party is the expensive mistake. Law firms are told they need a private model trained on their own data. I wanted to know whether that is true for this task, on a normal MacBook, before anyone pays for it.

How it was tested

  • Real documents, real answers: public federal complaints from the RECAP archive. The answer key is each court docket's own party list, not labels written by an AI.
  • A held-out test: 100 complaints from many courts for the test, 220 others for training, with near-copies of test cases removed.
  • Three contenders, one prompt: Qwen3-4B run locally in 4-bit, the same model after LoRA training on the 220 complaints (about two hours), and Claude Sonnet.

What it showed

The untrained 4B model on a laptop found 98.9% of parties against Claude's 99.2%, a little noisier on precision (90% against 93%). Training made it worse at what matters: tidier, but it missed more parties, sometimes got stuck repeating one name, and learned the docket's habit of leaving out Doe defendants. For this task the value of a private model is privacy, a free offline model that never sends client documents anywhere at near-Claude accuracy, not training on industry data. Training should pay off on firm-specific work, and only with labels that list every party.

How it was built

Built with Claude Code on my M2 MacBook: Claude collected the complaints, built the splits, ran the training with Apple's MLX and scored all three models. I set the question and the rules of the test, including that the answer key could not come from an AI.

items.title: Byzantium
items.lede: An illustrated encyclopedia of the Eastern Roman Empire, 324 to 1453, built around a mosaic atlas you can drag through 1,129 years and watch the borders move.
items.body_html:
Explore the live atlas

Dated territory snapshots
200
Map features
11,850
Encyclopedia entries
464
Licensed images
1,174
Podcast episodes indexed
440
Invalid geometries / overlaps
0 / 0

The atlas

Drawn as a mosaic

Territory is one fixed grid of tesserae, each slightly varied in shade, with grout between them. The empire is imperial purple edged in gold; the sea is blue tile. A Borders mode switches to clean outlines, and light and dark themes each have their own palette.

Conquest you can watch

When borders change, only the tiles that changed owner turn over, in a wave that starts from the conqueror's side, so territory is taken rather than repainted. Cities that change hands send out a ripple.

Built for scrubbing

Drag, click or use the keyboard; play at 1 to 50 years a second; or press Next change to jump to the next year the map moves. Ownership is cached per snapshot and neighbours precomputed, so fast scrubbing stays smooth.

Contested land stays contested

Overlapping claims of more than about 500 km² become hatched contested land instead of being handed to one side. Five places where the source disagrees with history, from Manzikert to 1453, are corrected and explained on the map.

Checked against the source

An automated check confirms zero invalid geometries and zero overlaps across all 200 snapshots, and ten key years match the source to within 1% of land area. Five other map sources were evaluated and rejected, each with a written reason.

More ways in

Compare two years side by side with a draggable divider, switch to a table of powers, toggle cities, battles and campaign routes, and share any view by its URL. Patterns stand in for colour, and reduced motion swaps flips for fades.

The encyclopedia around it

  • 464 entries pinned to fixed Wikipedia revisions with restored footnotes, plus 168 original introductions labelled as such.
  • 1,174 Commons images with author and licence; 41 were left out because their licence couldn't be confirmed.
  • A guide to all 440 episodes of The History of Byzantium podcast. The build fails if any 12-word run matches the podcast's pages.
  • 87 battle entries, a people index of 1,765, a gazetteer, coins, a primary-source reader for Procopius and Anna Komnene, and a timeline that shares its playhead with the atlas.

Built and verified

React, TypeScript and d3-geo, with Python pipelines for the map geometry: borders from the Seshat Cliopatria dataset, coastlines from Natural Earth, and 96 cities and 71 battles from Wikidata. It ships with 20 slider tests, 60 screenshot checks across phone and desktop, and Lighthouse mobile scores of 93 to 96.

How it was built

One long Claude Code session took it from an empty folder to a verified site. Claude evaluated map sources and their licences, built three data pipelines and the renderer, and wrote its own reports on what failed, what was skipped and where the sources disagree, for me to review.

items.title: ME/CFS and Long COVID evidence map
items.lede: Thousands of small studies have measured something in people with ME/CFS or Long COVID, and few results have been checked against each other. This project read the whole PubMed literature, pulled out every measured finding with its quote, and graded which ones independent labs have actually replicated.
items.body_html:
Research write-up

Abstracts screened
15,923
Studies in the database
1,981
Findings, each with its source quote
7,337
Findings graded strong (ME/CFS / Long COVID)
17 / 33
Brain tissues enriched in the genetics test
11 of 13

The problem

ME/CFS has been studied for decades and Long COVID has added thousands of papers in a few years, but most studies are small and many contradict each other. Nobody had pulled the whole literature into one table that says which findings hold up across independent labs and which do not.

What it does

  • Extracts every finding from each abstract: what was measured, in whom, against which comparison group, and in which direction, with the sentence it came from.
  • Grades replication by lab, not by paper, so a group publishing the same cohort five times counts once. Replicated nulls are kept too, such as the 11 of 11 labs that found no XMRV.
  • Compares the two illnesses side by side. Both show the same circulation and exercise picture: a racing heart on standing, a lower stroke volume and reduced peak oxygen uptake.

Predictions written down first

The replicated findings suggested an immune, vascular and autonomic chain. Before opening any genetic data, the predictions were written down and locked with a file hash, then tested against the open DecodeME genome study with MAGMA gene-set and tissue analysis. The signal sat in the brain: 11 of 13 brain tissues and the pituitary were enriched, which agrees with what the DecodeME team reported themselves.

How it was built

Built with Claude, under my direction, across several long Claude sessions. Claude wrote the search and grading code, ran the extraction in batches of 100 abstracts, audited its own output and ran the genetics pipeline. I directed the work and made the calls along the way, including writing the genetics predictions down before the test.

items.title: Clear Aftercare
items.lede: Discharge papers are written in abbreviations and handed to people who are tired, unwell or 80 years old. Paste them in and get a plain-language care sheet plus a calendar reminder for every dose, task and appointment, with anything unclear marked instead of guessed.
items.body_html:
Try the demoThe example and calendar buttons work on this site; reading new instructions runs inside Claude

What it does

  • Rewrites, never adds. Abbreviations become plain words, but the prompt forbids adding any medicine, dose, time, duration or advice that is not on the paper.
  • Flags the gaps: twice a day with no times, a dose in mg with no pill strength, "continue home meds" with no list, a follow-up nobody booked.
  • Turns on reminders only when they are complete. Calendar buttons switch on once times, start date and number of days are set, with one-click presets such as 8 AM and 8 PM.
  • Built for the reader: a large-text toggle, a dose checklist, a print view and a rough reading-grade score.
How it was built

Built with Claude as a single page that calls Claude to read the instructions. Claude wrote the page, the prompt, the calendar files and the example, and checked prior work in the field, under my direction.

items.title: Trauma guideline citation audit
items.lede: Military trauma guidelines tell medics and surgeons what to do, and each recommendation cites a paper. This audit checked whether the cited papers say what the guidelines claim, and found reference lists whose numbers had slipped out of line.
items.body_html:
Research write-up

What it found

  • Shifted reference numbers. In the pain, anxiety and delirium guideline, 24 of 27 wrong-topic citations fit the entry two numbers later, so the in-text numbers look keyed to a different list. The TBI neurosurgery guideline shows a shift of one in its later references.
  • Smaller slips elsewhere: two swapped references in one guideline and a reference reused for every cross-reference in another.
  • 56 specific citations are listed for a person to confirm by opening the PDF and reading the two entries.

Decisions behind it

  • Lead with what anyone can check. A shifted reference number is verifiable in minutes, so it is the headline, not a subjective "does this paper support it" grade.
  • Distrust the big number. AI grading flagged about 38% of citations as unsupported, but that fell to 18% when the full paper was available instead of the abstract, so it is reported as a likely overestimate.
  • Second opinion, labelled as such. ChatGPT re-graded 150 items and agreed closely with Claude (kappa 0.76).
How it was built

Built with Claude under my direction. Claude downloaded the guidelines, extracted every cited statement, matched each reference to PubMed, graded support and ran the reference-shift test; ChatGPT did the second-model check. The result is a list of specific, correctable errors in these guidelines.
